analysis.one_liner: Directs the FDA to set legal limits for lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in baby food and require testing.
analysis.headline: The Baby Food Safety Act of 2024, which would have required the FDA to set safety limits for lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in infant and toddler food and mandated company testing, died in committee without a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the FDA to set enforceable limits on four toxic heavy metals — lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury — in food made for babies and toddlers up to age two, and in fruit and vegetable purees and juices. Companies would have had to test their products at least quarterly, keep records the FDA could inspect, run environmental monitoring in their plants, and face mandatory recall authority if products exceeded the limits. It also tightened rules for imported food and added reporting on foreign food inspections.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and infants: the bill targeted the toxic metals that appear in store-bought baby food, which children's developing brains are most sensitive to. It also would have strengthened FDA oversight of imported foods held to the same standards as domestic ones, and given the agency power to force a recall of adulterated baby food rather than rely on voluntary action.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Parents and babies eating store-bought baby food

how_it_helps.text: Would have required the FDA to set binding limits on lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in infant and toddler food and in fruit and vegetable purees and juices, with proposed orders for lead and arsenic due by the end of 2025 and each limit reviewed at least every four years.

Would have required manufacturers to test samples of final products at least quarterly for these toxic elements, keep records for FDA inspection, and use accredited laboratories — so safety claims would rest on documented testing rather than company assurances.

Would have made any baby food exceeding the limits legally adulterated, giving the FDA mandatory recall authority over such food and creating a prohibited act for failing the testing, recordkeeping, or records-production requirements.
Would have required environmental pathogen monitoring in baby food plants and strengthened FDA access to records in advance of or in lieu of on-site inspections, including for imported food.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of infant and toddler food and of fruit and vegetable purees and juices would bear the cost of testing, recordkeeping, and plant monitoring (the bill puts records provision at the company's expense), and some of that cost could show up in prices. The FDA would take on new rulemaking, testing, and inspection work. Food importers would face new record-verification duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Baby food makers, puree and juice processors, importers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on manufacturers — quarterly accredited-lab testing, written sampling plans, and environmental monitoring programs — and some of that cost would likely be passed to consumers through slightly higher baby food prices.

The deadlines were ambitious: proposed limits for lead and arsenic were due by December 31, 2025 and mercury by 2028, and heavy metals occur naturally in soil and crops, so setting limits 'at the level at which the contaminant may render the food injurious to health' while accounting for unavoidable contamination would have been technically difficult and open to challenge.
The bill exempted infant formula from its definition of infant or toddler food, so formula — a major part of many babies' diets — would not have been covered by these specific contaminant limits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — enforceable limits on neurotoxic heavy metals in food aimed at infants and toddlers, with real testing and recall teeth — was large and the direct costs, mostly borne by a concentrated food-manufacturing industry, were modest relative to it. The main design weaknesses were tight rulemaking deadlines and the difficulty of scientifically setting limits for naturally occurring contaminants, and the formula exemption left one significant product category out. On balance this was a well-aimed consumer safety bill whose cost of never being considered fell on the families it would have protected.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi introduced the bill on July 23, 2024, with Rep. Tony Cárdenas as the original cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce that same day.
That referral was the last action of any kind: the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and it expired with the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of infant and toddler food avoided new testing, recordkeeping, and contaminant-limit compliance costs, since the bill was never taken up. Babies and parents gained nothing, because no contaminant limits were set.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Baby food manufacturers, which avoided new compliance costs

for.name: Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Baby Food Safety Act of 2024 on July 23, 2024.

for.name: Tony Cárdenas
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Chair Cathy McMorris Rodgers)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured; the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were both Democrats, and the committee that declined to act was chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed binding heavy-metal limits, quarterly accredited-lab testing of final products, extensive recordkeeping, and environmental pathogen monitoring in plants — a real compliance cost. Its interest in avoiding those costs ran against the interest of parents in lower contaminant levels in food sold for babies.

industries.industry: Fruit and vegetable puree and juice processors
industries.note: The bill's contaminant limits and testing requirements would have covered foods predominantly composed of fruit or vegetable puree or juice, not just branded baby food, extending the compliance burden across a broader slice of the food industry.
Mandatory quarterly testing in accredited labs would have created steady new demand for commercial food-testing services.

Importers would have had to monitor and verify the accuracy of manufacturers' testing records, and the bill directed a study and better reporting on whether imported food is inspected at the same level as domestic food.
